name: Agipo
classification_notes: Elementary grotesque with selective geometric inflections. Flat 90° terminals give a mechanical quality; tall x-height and very short descenders produce a dense, graphic texture. Deliberately not a revival — Peško identified a small set of glyphs (the G, 1, y, r) to make distinctly odd within an otherwise restrained skeleton. Two stylistic sets (Southern/round and Northern/square) offer regional character alternates. Sits between Franklin Gothic-style grotesque and geometric traditions without fully committing to either.
summary: An elementary grotesque by Radim Peško, built on flat 90° terminals and a tight x-height, with two regional stylistic sets and a handful of quietly eccentric glyphs that distinguish it within an otherwise plain structure.
description: Agipo occupies the ground between grotesque and geometric without belonging wholly to either. Peško's approach was selective: most characters are restrained and workhorse-plain, while a few — the G, the 1, the y — are made deliberately distinct, giving designers a recognisable scaffold with something to show. The family covers Latin and Cyrillic in three weights with italics, plus Mono, Extended and Condensed cuts, and two stylistic sets (Southern round, Northern square) that shift the texture of a text block without changing the typeface.
foundry_blurb: Agipo is an elementary sans serif with a plain character, available in three weights with italics and three additional styles. Its character set covers a wide range of Latin and Cyrillic languages. Two stylistic sets — Southern (round) and Northern (square) — contain alternative characters and punctuation that gently colour text like a regional accent.

name: A Gothic
classification_notes: A contemporary grotesque in the American gothic tradition. Spans Latin, Cyrillic and Greek scripts across 80-plus languages. The companion AA Gothic family applies an inverted ink trap principle for display use, cutting into junctions rather than opening them to sharpen character at headline scale.
summary: A two-weight grotesque with italics covering Latin, Cyrillic and Greek, designed over five years alongside a companion display family that inverts the ink trap concept for headline use.
description: A Gothic comes in Regular and Bold weights with matching italics, covering more than 80 languages across Latin, Cyrillic and Greek scripts. Its companion set, AA Gothic, reverses the conventional ink trap logic – cutting into junctions rather than opening them – making those styles suited to titles, headings and inscriptions. Developed between 2014 and 2019, the pair reflects Pesko's characteristic approach: formally rigorous, with a clear conceptual framework behind each design decision.
foundry_blurb: A Gothic is drawn in two weights with italics and a complementary AA Gothic set. The AA styles reverse the traditional ink trap idea – originally devised so that removed areas absorb ink spread at small sizes – making them suited to titles, headings and inscriptions instead. Like dents du bonheur, those cuts give the typeface its distinctive detail and personality.

name: Correspondance
classification_notes: Single-weight, uppercase-only geometric display sans-serif. Drawn from memory of Adrian Frutiger's lettering for the Paris Metro signage system rather than traced from source material, giving it a subtly hand-interpreted character despite its geometric structure. Alternate versions exist for select characters. Strictly a display face: no lowercase, no text weights.
summary: A single-weight, uppercase-only geometric display sans-serif reconstructed from Peško's memory of Frutiger's Paris Metro signage lettering.
description: Correspondance is Radim Peško's recollection of the lettering Frutiger designed for the Paris Metro, rebuilt without reference. That distinction matters: the result carries the flatness of institutional signage filtered through subjective recall, giving it a quality no straight revival could produce. One weight, one case – its constraints are its character.
foundry_blurb: RP Digital Type Foundry, operating since 2001, was founded by Radim Peško. The foundry describes its purpose as creating typefaces as monuments to those overlooked by history and invisible in the present.

name: Dear Sir Madam
classification_notes: Calligraphic display type rooted in sign-writing tradition. References Eric Gill's facia lettering, Edward Johnston's alphabets and E.M. Catich's inscriptional studies. Straight lines are deliberately reduced to preserve an organic, hand-drawn weight. Roman capitals with a humanist, pre-industrial sensibility.
summary: A calligraphic display type drawn from sign-writing tradition – originally made for exhibition labels in 2011, distributed privately to collaborators, and released publicly in 2023.
description: Dear Sir Madam began as a bespoke typeface for the "Zak Kyes Working With..." exhibition in 2011, sent to contributors as an invitation-only font – which is where the name comes from. The design draws from inscriptional sources: Eric Gill's facia lettering, Johnston's alphabets and E.M. Catich's studies, keeping organic, calligraphic qualities intact by minimising straight lines and embracing inconsistencies rather than correcting them. Roman and Italic styles come with 12 stylistic sets of alternates, giving it real flexibility for editorial and display use.
foundry_blurb: Dear Sir Madam was conceived for exhibition object labels and wall texts, drawing on classical shapes used as guides for sign-writers. The design minimises straight lines to preserve its organic, calligraphic character, embracing imperfections rather than eliminating them. Originally distributed as a personal-use font to each contributor to the exhibition, it is now available to all in Roman and Italic with twelve stylistic sets.

name: F Grotesk
classification_notes: Revival of Breite halbfette Grotesk and Französische Grotesk, two anonymous 19th-century German sans-serifs. Shares lineage with FF Bau but is more idiosyncratic in texture. Upright and italic across four weights with tabular and proportional figures.
summary: A revival of anonymous 19th-century German grotesques, drawn with enough irregularity and conviction to stand apart from the cleaner, more calibrated genre entries.
description: F Grotesk is rooted in Breite halbfette Grotesk and Französische Grotesk, two historical sans-serifs Pesko worked into a coherent contemporary family between 2007 and 2011. Four weights with matching italics, plus tabular and proportional figures, make it genuinely functional across editorial, identity and institutional settings. The letterforms carry a lively, slightly uneven quality that reads as craft rather than accident.
foundry_blurb: F Grotesk has boldly drawn forms that work across a wide range of sizes and applications, with a singular and lively appearance that connects it to anonymous late 19th-century sans serif design.

name: Boymans
classification_notes: Modular geometric display typeface inspired by Lance Wyman's 1968 Mexico City Olympic Games typeface. Ten weights each available in three line-rendering variants (single, double and triple line), giving 30 styles in total plus a New Block variant. Designed as a custom commission for the Mevis & Van Deursen identity for Museum Boijmans van Beuningen in Rotterdam. Not available for commercial licensing.
summary: A modular geometric display face designed in 2003 for Museum Boijmans van Beuningen, built across ten weights each in single, double and triple line variants that can be layered or coloured for a wide range of typographic combinations.
description: Commissioned by Mevis & Van Deursen for the Museum Boijmans van Beuningen identity, Boymans takes its structural cues from Lance Wyman's 1968 Mexico City Olympics typeface. Ten weights, each available in single, double and triple line versions, produce 30 styles in total; layering or colouring these variants generates near-endless typographic combinations. The face is not available for commercial licensing.
foundry_blurb: Boymans was originally designed in 2003 as part of the identity for Museum Boijmans van Beuningen in Rotterdam. Built across ten weights with single-line, double-line and triple-line versions per weight, it offers a flexible and playful system in which combining, layering or colouring the variants generates an endless range of typographic possibilities.

name: AA Gothic
classification_notes: Display-weight grotesque sans designed as the headline complement to A Gothic. Its defining device is inverted ink traps: rather than removing corner material to aid ink spread at small sizes, the design adds deliberate notched corners that function as a visual signature at large scale. Structurally orthodox grotesque construction otherwise, with the same skeleton as A Gothic.
summary: A display companion to A Gothic that inverts the ink trap device, turning corner notches from an optical correction into the typeface's defining mark at headline scale.
description: AA Gothic pairs with Peško's A Gothic as its display counterpart, sharing the same grotesque skeleton but flipping the ink trap logic: rather than removing corner material to assist ink spread at small sizes, the design adds deliberate notches that become its visual signature when set large. The conceit works because it subverts something normally invisible, making a functional device into a point of character. Two weights, Regular and Bold, cover Latin, Cyrillic and Greek across more than sixty languages.
foundry_blurb: AA Gothic is a companion set to A Gothic, reversing the idea of ink traps – a device originally conceived for small sizes, where ink spread into removed corner areas – so that those structural notches instead provide personality and distinction in titles, headings and inscriptions.

name: Girott
classification_notes: Subtractive compressed sans-serif. Letterforms are derived by cutting rather than constructing – a reductive approach that produces tight, angular shapes with strong vertical stress and minimal stroke contrast. The compressed proportions orient it towards display use, though it works well in editorial headlines. Two-weight only: Regular and Bold. Broad Latin and Cyrillic coverage including Bulgarian alternates.
summary: A compressed, subtractive sans-serif in two weights, built on a reductive formal logic that carves letterforms rather than constructs them.
description: Designed over four years from 2012 to 2016, Girott applies a subtractive design principle – shapes carved out rather than drawn – producing a compressed sans with a precise, near-industrial character. The two-weight family handles display and editorial headline use well, with broad Latin and Cyrillic coverage including Bulgarian alternates. Pesko's conceptual rigour gives it a clarity rare among compressed grotesques.
foundry_blurb: Girott is a compressed subtractive typeface whose tight shapes were cut in two weights, Regular and Bold. The foundry sums it up in three words: cut, stable, sans.

name: Larish Alte
classification_notes: Single-weight display serif with roots in early 20th-century Austrian lettering, specifically Rudolf von Larisch's calligraphic prints and books. Two OpenType stylistic sets alter the lowercase 'a', uppercase 'A', and 'y', shifting its character between variants. Distinctive letterforms — particularly the uppercase R — give it an ornamental quality suited to headline and identity work rather than extended body text. Features lining and old-style figures, several ligatures, and an Interfinity mark.
summary: A single-weight display serif drawn from Rudolf von Larisch's early 20th-century Austrian lettering, with two OpenType stylistic sets that shift its personality and a distinctive ornamental quality well suited to cultural and editorial contexts.
description: Larish Alte was originally drawn in 2006 for the Secession contemporary art space in Vienna, then redrawn and published by Radim Peško's RP Digital Type Foundry. It comes in a single semibold weight with two stylistic sets offering alternate forms for the lowercase 'a', uppercase 'A', and 'y' — a small switch with a noticeable effect on tone. Its letterforms, particularly the uppercase R, sit at the ornamental end of the serif spectrum, making it a natural fit for headline work, cultural identities, and editorial display settings.
foundry_blurb: Originally commissioned for Vienna's Secession art space in 2006, Larish Alte takes Rudolf von Larisch's early 20th-century prints and books as its starting point. The typeface was subsequently redrawn and extended with new details, gaining OpenType support for two stylistic sets, lining and old-style figures, ligatures, and an Interfinity mark. It has appeared in headlines for the Austrian newspaper Der Standard.

name: Lÿno
classification_notes: Four-style family sharing a consistent stroke weight but operating on entirely distinct formal logic per style. Jean was built from cardboard offcuts via a Dada-inflected cut-and-photograph process; Walt fuses Futura's geometric vectors with the hand-lettered flow of Waltograph; Stan references Kubrick's visual world; Ulys draws on a French-Japanese animated series. No italic or condensed cuts exist. Each style is essentially its own typeface, connected by weight rather than letterform genealogy.
summary: A four-style experimental display family co-designed by Karl Nawrot and Radim Pesko between 2009 and 2012, each style named after a cultural figure and built on a shared stroke weight but a completely different formal logic.
description: Lÿno's four styles – Jean, Stan, Ulys and Walt – take their names from Jean Arp, Stanley Kubrick, Ulysses 31 and Walt Disney, each channelling a different typographic sensibility. Walt merges Futura's geometric rigour with the hand-lettered flow of Waltograph; Jean was constructed from cardboard offcuts photographed and digitised in a process closer to Dada collage than type design. All four share a consistent weight of line, giving them a coherent visual family despite their divergent personalities.
foundry_blurb: The characters negotiate the digital freedoms of their production through playful typologies of form – open and various, built expressly to resist normative tendencies and reject the idea of definitive form.

name: Larish Neue
classification_notes: Descended from the rejected experimental drafts Peško produced alongside Larish Alte in 2006, which itself digitised Rudolf von Larisch's 1903 humanist serif Plinius for the Vienna Secession. Larish Neue uses entirely different construction principles from Larish Alte – the historical DNA reads only on close inspection – and arrives at something more contemporary and assertive. Limited to a single Semibold weight with accompanying Italic; designed for headline and display use rather than text.
summary: A contemporary display serif built from the Vienna Secession's rejected drafts, carrying the faint genetic trace of a 1903 Viennese humanist into something sharper and wholly its own.
description: Larish Neue began as the road not taken during Peško's 2006 Larish Alte revival – experimental letterforms the Vienna Secession passed on, reworked on different construction principles into a standalone release in 2011. The connection to its Plinius ancestor is present but buried; what reads on the surface is a confident, slightly idiosyncratic serif with character in the details, particularly the lowercase f. With only a Semibold and its Italic, it is a narrow tool – but one with genuine point of view, used to strong effect by Pitchfork, Sternberg Press and Jay-Z's visual identity team.
foundry_blurb: A by-product of Larish Alte. The version emerged from an attempt to produce a contemporary-looking typeface that carries the DNA of the original, built on entirely different construction principles – the historical lineage visible only upon close inspection.

name: Kin
classification_notes: All-caps display typeface — caps and small caps only — in a single weight with no italic. The defining structural decision is that diacritical marks are welded into the body of each letterform rather than floating above or below as separate components. Designed purely for headline use; no text variant exists.
summary: A single-weight all-caps display face by Radim Pesko, designed over nearly three years in London, with diacritical marks structurally built into each letterform rather than placed as floating components.
description: Kin was designed in London between 2017 and 2020, offering caps and small capitals in a single weight with no italic and no text companion. Its defining characteristic is the treatment of diacritics: each accent is welded directly into the body of the letter, giving the face a unified, dense texture suited to headline settings. It covers Latin script across more than 60 languages and was used in headlines at Le Monde.
foundry_blurb: Designed in London between April 2017 and January 2020, with pronounced diacritics welded into the letter shapes. Kin consists of caps and small caps in a single style and weight, covering Latin script only.

name: Fugue
classification_notes: Geometric sans-serif built as an explicit dialogue with Paul Renner's work. Strong circular forms and extremely low stroke contrast place it close to the Futura tradition, though with distinctive moves: a characteristic lowercase g, a capital I with bars, and stylistic alternates for double-storey 'a' and 't' in the italic. Originally designed solely at 12pt text size; the 2016 additions of Head and the subsequent Tails variant extended it into display use.
summary: A single-weight geometric sans grown from a 12pt text commission into a five-style system with monospace, display and Cyrillic range, rooted in a deliberate reckoning with Paul Renner.
description: Fugue was developed for the Werkplaats Typografie tenth anniversary book in 2008, conceived as a formal conversation with Paul Renner's geometric tradition. Strong circular forms, very low stroke contrast and a capital I with bars give it a precise, industrial character; stylistic alternates in the italic allow a more humanist double-storey 'a' and 't'. The family has since grown to five styles, including a monospace and the display-oriented Tails variant, with Latin and Cyrillic coverage across more than 30 languages.
foundry_blurb: Peško describes Fugue as an appreciation of – and a return trip through – Paul Renner's geometric thinking. First used in the Werkplaats Typografie anniversary publication of 2008 and originally conceived for twelve-point setting only, the family now spans Regular, Italic, Monospace and the headline-focused Tails style, supporting Latin and Cyrillic scripts across over 30 languages.

name: Paabo
classification_notes: Strictly geometric construction based on circular forms, with deliberate non-Euclidean disruptions built into the design logic. Thirteen stylistic variants span functional text weights through highly decorative display cuts. Sits within the mid-century geometric tradition but with a contemporary, idiosyncratic sensibility that sets it apart from purely rationalist designs.
summary: A geometric sans-serif with thirteen stylistic variants built on circular construction, from clean functional weights to wilfully eccentric display cuts, with Latin, Greek and Cyrillic support.
description: Paabo's geometry takes a ball-game premise seriously: circular forms dominate, with occasional deliberate disruptions the designer describes as non-Euclidean. The thirteen styles run from workable text weights (Regular, Bold) through optical experiments (Round, Soap, Outline) to outright display oddities like Goggles, Pinball and Quadrat. Latin, Greek and Cyrillic support make it more broadly deployable than its playful exterior suggests.
foundry_blurb: A typeface as simple as a ball game, built on strictly geometric construction and occasionally broken by what Pesko calls the flight of a non-Euclidean fly.

name: Mitim
classification_notes: A text serif built on a distinctive triangular (three-point) serif structure, designed at a semibold weight equivalent and calibrated for reading at text sizes. Developed as a bespoke commission for Dot Dot Dot magazine (issues 11–20), with each Greek-letter-named iteration (Alpha through Lambda) redesigned in direct response to a new issue's theme, context and production conditions. Not a conventional type release – an iterative typographic project sustained across a decade of editorial publishing. Not available for licensing. Type field: foundry.
summary: A bespoke text serif built on triangular serifs, developed across eleven Greek-letter-named iterations for Dot Dot Dot magazine between 2005 and 2011.
description: Commissioned specifically for Dot Dot Dot magazine, Mitim evolved through eleven iterations from Alpha to Lambda, each redesigned in response to a new issue's context, theme and production conditions. The constant across all versions is the triangular serif structure and a semibold weight calibrated for reading at text sizes. Unavailable for licensing, it stands as one of the more rigorously documented examples of typeface design as a sustained editorial project.
foundry_blurb: Mitim is an ongoing project designed around a specific brief for Dot Dot Dot magazine, defined throughout by its triangular serifs. The family grows and changes with each new issue in response to shifting production conditions – context, theme, approach and spirit, as well as production constraints and the needs of individual contributions.

name: Merkury
classification_notes: Rounded geometric sans-serif with softly closed apertures and a distinctively oversized dot on the i. Originally named Mercury; renamed Merkury to avoid confusion with H&Co's Mercury and Fountain's similarly named face. Includes a monospaced variant based on the Medium weight. Cyrillic support includes specialised character alternates for Bulgarian and Macedonian.
summary: A rounded sans-serif from Radim Pesko, sketched in 2001 and refined over two decades, offered in four weights with matching italics, a monospaced variant and broad Latin and Cyrillic coverage.
description: Merkury originated as sketches for the 2001 group exhibition 'From Mars: Self-initiated Projects in Graphic Design', and was refined over subsequent years before settling into its current form. Its rounded strokes and oversized dot on the i give it a soft but precise character – sitting at the gentle end of the geometric sans tradition without tipping into novelty. A Mono variant extends its usefulness into code and tabular settings, while Cyrillic support comes with specialised alternates for Bulgarian and Macedonian.
foundry_blurb: First sketched in 2001 for the exhibition 'From Mars: Self-initiated Projects in Graphic Design', Merkury (originally written as Mercury) underwent successive rounds of refinement and customisation before reaching its current form. Pesko describes the typeface as defined by its curious rounded character.

name: Renotype
classification_notes: Low-contrast sans-serif conceived as a formal archetype for the Latin alphabet, designed without reference to any specific epoch or tool. The family expands laterally through five conceptually distinct stylistic registers — Regular, Italic, Mono, Quasitalic and Medieval — rather than a conventional weight axis. Mono variant confirms the grotesque/geometric base construction. OpenType features include case-sensitive forms, discretionary and standard ligatures, tabular figures, slashed zero, ordinals and arrows.
summary: A low-contrast Latin archetype by Radim Peško, released in 2024 after seven years of development, with five conceptually distinct styles that expand the family through formal registers rather than a conventional weight axis.
description: Renotype distils the Latin alphabet to a functional core, with letterforms designed without reference to any specific era or tool. Five styles — Regular, Italic, Mono, Quasitalic and Medieval — expand the family not through weight but through distinct formal registers, from the conventional to the fictionalized. Developed over seven years in collaboration with French foundry 205TF, where it is licensed, the family supports over 200 languages across extended Latin and Greek character sets.
foundry_blurb: Peško describes Renotype as a simple, low-contrast typeface designed to serve as an archetype or mould for Latin letterforms — shapes that are "aesthetically functional, like a bathroom," free from any specific historical period or tool. The five styles establish different narrative registers: traditional (Regular, Italic), standardised (Mono), playful (Quasitalic) and speculative (Medieval), each suggesting further typographic possibilities beyond the family itself.

name: Union
classification_notes: A deliberate synthesis of Helvetica and Arial, adjusting the contours of both to produce a neutral grotesque that sits between the two. No optical sizes or width variants; the concept is the distinguishing feature rather than any structural novelty in the letterforms.
summary: A grotesque that deliberately synthesises Helvetica and Arial, occupying the ambiguous middle ground between the two dominant platform typefaces of the digital era.
description: Designed in 2009, Union merges the contours of Helvetica and Arial into a single grotesque that belongs fully to neither. It is intended for situations where Helvetica reads as too considered and Arial as too blunt — a genuinely specific brief that gives the face a coherent identity rather than a merely generic one. Available in two weights with italics, it has been used across editorial, cultural institution and branding work.
foundry_blurb: Union derives from the two most commonly used typefaces on PC and Mac platforms — Arial and Helvetica. Its contours are adjusted to retain the flexibility characteristic of both, for moments where one feels too sophisticated and the other too vulgar.

name: Union SMA
classification_notes: Display extension of the Union grotesque family, commissioned exclusively for Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam's visual identity. Union is itself a conceptual synthesis of Arial and Helvetica; the SMA variant adapts those letterforms into bespoke display cuts for institutional use. Not available for licensing.
summary: Bespoke display extensions of Peško's Union grotesque, drawn for Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam's visual identity in 2012 and not available for licensing.
description: Union SMA extends Radim Peško's Union typeface into a set of custom display styles made for the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam. The base Union is itself a conceptual piece: a synthesis of Arial and Helvetica, occupying the territory between their respective cultural registers. The SMA cuts translate that framework into dedicated display letterforms for one of Europe's foremost contemporary art institutions.
foundry_blurb: Union SMA is a series of custom display styles developed for the visual identity of Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam, released in 2012. The typeface is not available for licensing.

name: Sol
classification_notes: Highly abstract modular display typeface where each letterform is constructed from cubic wireframe structures, derived from Sol LeWitt's 1974 sculptural series. Letters are not conventionally legible but recognisable through spatial inference – the viewer must locate them within geometric compositions. Two material variants (Steel, Wood) reference the physical qualities of LeWitt's source artwork.
summary: Sol draws letterforms out of the cubic spatial logic of Sol LeWitt's 1974 incomplete-open-cube series, producing abstract compositions in two material variants – Steel and Wood – that require the viewer to resolve letter from structure.
description: Each glyph in Sol is derived from the spatial possibilities of a cube, continuing LeWitt's 1974 artwork '122 variations on incomplete open cubes' as typographic practice. The two variants – Steel and Wood – carry the material language of LeWitt's source structures into the character set. The typeface is not available for commercial licensing and has appeared editorially in New York Times Style headlines.
foundry_blurb: Sol extends Sol LeWitt's 1974 project – 122 views of unfinished cubes built from wooden planks – into a typeface whose character set is defined by the spatial potential of a cube. The new letterforms are not given directly; they depend on the viewer's imagination and ability to identify letters within what reads, at first, as abstract composition.

name: Septima
classification_notes: Single-weight monospaced typeface with asymmetrical letterforms individually calibrated to each glyph window for even optical tone. Not a conventional grid-based mono — the asymmetry is a deliberate design instrument, not a quirk.
summary: A single-weight monospaced typeface whose asymmetrical letterforms are individually calibrated to the glyph window, producing even optical weight and distinctly recognisable characters across Latin and Cyrillic scripts.
description: Septima is built around a precise internal logic: each letterform is adjusted to the space it occupies in the glyph window, keeping optical weight consistent while giving every character a strong individual presence. It covers twenty-three Latin languages and six Cyrillic languages, with the Cyrillic developed in collaboration with Roman Gornitsky. BBC News has used it in headline settings, which is a reasonable measure of its legibility under pressure.
foundry_blurb: Septima's letterforms are asymmetrical by design — each is calibrated to the space it occupies in the glyph window so that every character carries equal tone while remaining distinctly recognisable. Latin and Cyrillic are both supported; the Cyrillic was developed in collaboration with Roman Gornitsky.
